title: What the prayer says
told: a saying of the Prophet ﷺ

hook.say: before the story, can i ask you something? is there something you’ve said a hundred times without ever stopping to think what it means?
options: then you’ll love this one. listen.
then this story is very close to home. listen.
keep listening. you might find one by the end.

steps.line: In the simple mosque in Medina, roofed with palm branches, a man named Abu Sa‘id was praying when the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ called his name.

steps.q: He’s in the middle of his prayer, and the Prophet ﷺ calls him. What do you think he does?
o: Cuts his prayer short and comes
steps.why: He finished first. The Prophet ﷺ then gently reminded him of a verse: answer God and His Messenger when he calls you (8:24).

steps.line: He finished his prayer, then came over. The Prophet ﷺ told him, “Before you leave the mosque, I will teach you the greatest surah, the greatest chapter, of the Qur’an.”
They walked toward the door together. Just before they reached it, Abu Sa‘id spoke up: “You said you would teach me.”

steps.q: The greatest surah. Which one do you think it is?
steps.why: Al-Ikhlas is said to equal a third of the Qur’an, and the Throne Verse is called its greatest verse. But the greatest surah is the one in every prayer: al-Fatiha.

steps.line: “Praise be to God, Lord of the worlds,” he answered. “It is the seven oft-repeated verses.” Al-Fatiha: the opening.

steps.q: The prayer starts by talking about God. Which line first talks to Him?
o: “Praise be to God, Lord of the worlds”
steps.why: The first verses speak about God: Lord, Most Merciful, Master of the Day. Then it turns and speaks straight to Him: “You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help.”

steps.line: In another saying, the Prophet ﷺ said God answers as you pray. When someone says, “Praise be to God, Lord of the worlds,” God says, “My servant has praised Me.”

steps.q: If God answers as you pray it, what changes when you know what its lines mean?
o: You can follow your own side of it
steps.why: In a hadith, God says, “I have divided the prayer between Me and My servant.” Knowing the words lets you hear both halves.

steps.q: In the hadith, God answers each line. Match the line to the answer.
pairs: “You alone we worship, You alone we ask”
“This is between Me and My servant”
“My servant shall have what he asked”
steps.why: This hadith qudsi is in Sahih Muslim. The middle line is shared: worship from us, help from Him. The last line is a request, and it is granted.

say: here’s what i love. the greatest surah is one of the shortest. seven lines, and every muslim who prays says it many times a day.
in islam, there’s no prayer without it. it’s mostly praise, it asks for one thing, the straight path, and God answers as you pray.

steps.q: Fatiha comes from a root meaning “to open.” From the lesson, why is that a fitting name?
o: It was the first surah ever revealed
It opens the Qur’an, and it opens every prayer
It was taught at a door, so it was named after it
steps.why: It’s the first surah of the Qur’an, and it opens every unit of every prayer. A key in Arabic, miftah, shares the same root.

today.say: pick one line of al-Fatiha and learn what it means: “show us the straight path.” it’s your choice: just read it, listen for it when someone prays, or say it yourself.
options: one line, known by heart in meaning. that’s how the whole prayer opens up.
beautiful. next time you hear it, you’ll know what’s being asked.

sources: Sahih al-Bukhari 4474 (Abu Sa‘id ibn al-Mu‘alla: called while praying, the promise to teach the greatest surah before leaving the mosque, “al-hamdu lillahi rabbil-‘alamin … the seven oft-repeated”)
Sahih Muslim 395 (hadith qudsi: the prayer divided between God and His servant, “My servant has praised Me”)
Sahih al-Bukhari 756; Sahih Muslim 394 (no prayer without al-Fatiha)
Sahih al-Bukhari 446 (the Prophet’s mosque: mud brick, a roof of palm leaves, pillars of palm trunks)
Qur’an 96:1–5 (the first verses revealed; the hard one’s wrong answer)
check: In Bukhari 4474 the Prophet ﷺ also reminds him of the verse about answering when called (8:24); the lesson leaves that out and only says he came “a little late”. Confirm that’s fair.
Muslim 395 lists God’s answers from “Praise be to God” onward (not the bismillah), so the lesson says “God answers as you pray”, not “every line”. Confirm.
The verse count follows the common numbering with the bismillah as verse 1 (same note as the day-2 script).
“There’s no prayer without it”: the Hanafi school treats al-Fatiha as wajib rather than a pillar (same note as the script). The teach line reports the hadith only.
